Subject guide

Live art programs and craft workshops

Explore drawing, painting, pottery, and other crafts. Compare the techniques, materials, and experience needed before choosing a program.

Explore current programs↗

Choose the thing you want to make

Start with the material or technique that interests you: drawing, painting, pottery, calligraphy, or another craft. Then look at the actual outcomes. A program about drawing faces asks something different of you than a general introduction to sketching. A useful listing tells you what you will practise and what experience you need.

Choose online or in person

An online program can let you work at your own table while watching a live demonstration. An in-person workshop may make more sense when the work calls for studio equipment or close physical guidance. Check the location, tools, and materials before choosing. Do not assume that supplies, firing, or finishing services are included unless the program says so.

Leave space for practice

A single workshop gives you a focused introduction. A program or lesson series can give you more time between sessions to try a technique again. Read the full schedule and think about when you will practise. If your provider shares program files or invites discussion, use those spaces to keep your questions connected to the program.

Look closely at the provider’s work

The portfolio is a useful place to start. Notice the materials, style, and type of work the provider shares, then read their background and the program requirements. If you are new, look for a beginner level and an explanation of what to bring. Ask about anything that would change your decision before you book.

Before you choose

A few things to check

  • The technique and level
  • Supplies you need to bring
  • Studio access or equipment
  • What the sessions cover

Current programs, prices, and dates are available in the app.

Choosing your program

Good questions
to ask.

Do I need to buy art supplies first?

Read the materials list before buying anything. The provider should explain what you need and whether any supplies are included. If a tool or material is unclear, ask about the specific program.

Can I learn a hands-on skill online?

Some techniques work well through live demonstrations and practice at home. Others depend on equipment or a physical workspace. Choose the delivery mode that fits the skill and the materials available to you.
